To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the location of a real bar is mislocalized when subjects briefly feel it while moving their hand across it.
Subjects systematically mislocalize a real object that is felt while moving ones hand over it.
subjects mislocalize a real bar that is briefly felt while moving ones hand over it.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the interaction between vision and touch.
the way humans perceive and act upon objects in the real world.
how we perceive our body and the world in relation to each other.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the human brain is not able to combine information about a stimulus and the movement of the sensory organs accurately and that this error in the combination of sensory information is a real-world property of human perception.

the mislocalization of a real object is not only a property of a visual or haptic stimulus presented briefly around the onset of a movement but also a property of a real object that is felt briefly while the hand is moved across it.

the brain combines visual, tactile and proprioceptive information in a manner that leads to systematic errors in the localization of visual and haptically presented stimuli, and that this error is also present when subjects feel real static objects while moving the hand across them.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have shown that movement-related mis-localization is a robust phenomenon in human perception.
we show that mislocalization of visual and haptical stimuli is a robust and general phenomenon, and that it is present in the real world, not just in a laboratory.
the human brain combines information from different senses in a way that is not optimal for the task at hand.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the brain combines sensory information with proprioceptive information, which leads to a systematic mislocalization of the sensory input.
we should be cautious about the interpretation of studies on the combination of visual and tactile information with proprioceptive information, because they might be influenced by a systematic bias.
the human brain is not a perfect machine.
